prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs experiments in first place and optical lattice clocks second, and after reading the other seven ballots I now put the clocks first. The scientific case is concrete: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light-shift problem, and Ye's group (with others) turned it into the most precise measurement devices ever built, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, relativistic geodesy, bounds on drifting constants and a credible route to redefining the second. The performance has been reproduced independently in strontium and ytterbium in several national laboratories and compared across continents, so maturity is not in doubt. It is also the only shortlisted entry that all eight members ranked (seven of them in the top three, two in first place, none below fourth), which tells me it is the entry with the least dependence on any one member's field. Its attribution is the cleanest on the list: one conceptual inventor and one leading experimental realiser, two names, no forced exclusion.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize ion control, so a sceptic can call optical lattice clocks a refinement of recognised metrology rather than a new discovery. The practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, has not happened yet, and ion-clock groups and several lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Lisdat and Sterr, Takamoto) have claims the two names do not reflect. Against my own opening choice: the Higgs discovery is scientifically the larger result and the experimental half has gone unrecognised since 2013, so passing over it for a cleaner but narrower prize has a real cost.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked the Higgs discovery only fifth because credit belongs to two collaborations of thousands and choosing three of four credited names is arbitrary; he also notes that the clocks have a clean allocation.
responses.response: I agree with the diagnosis more than my own opening ballot did. I picked Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni and called it defensible, but the seven ballots that ranked the Higgs entry proposed three different trios (Danielsson and Kroll omit Della Negra, Pearce and Eriksson omit Jenni, Johansson, Olsson and I omit Virdee), which shows that the evidence we have does not pick a trio. Where I differ from Eriksson is that arbitrary credit is a reason to find a defensible configuration, not to drop the science. I keep B001 as my first alternative and would support it if the committee can agree on a principled rule, such as the ATLAS and CMS founding leaders plus one spokesperson, rather than the leader-based trio any of us happens to remember.

responses.point: Kroll put optical lattice clocks first and disclosed a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, where Jun Ye is associated, as a possible perceived tie rather than a documented conflict.
responses.response: I accept Kroll's physics: the concept is clear, the realisation is decisive and the interpretation is stable. His disclosure matters for how the committee weighs his first place, so I would ask that his support be counted with that in mind, but the case does not depend on his ballot because Danielsson, Johansson and I ranked it second and Olsson and Pearce third. I do not agree with his reading that the 2005 comb prize makes timing more natural; that prize is also the best argument that the field has already been honoured, and I would want the citation to name the lattice idea and the 1e-18 performance, not the comb. His view of B054 as a clean second also seems fair to me, and I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Johansson ranked the Higgs discovery first and clocks second, but disclosed that circuit QED is close to his own work and WACQT and ranked it only fifth to compensate, and he also worries that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits is too close.
responses.response: I respect the disclosure, but I think the compensation may be too strong. I ranked circuit QED third and see it as a different discovery from the macroscopic quantum tunnelling honoured in 2025: strong single-photon coupling and dispersive readout is the architecture of the processors, not the tunnelling effect. That does not move it above clocks for me, because the 2025 proximity is a real worry and the Girvin omission leaves the attribution weaker than for B013. I would keep B054 as a live alternative and ask Johansson to state how he would weigh it without his own proximity.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the Higgs first and clocks second, and flagged the 2005 recognition of frequency-comb work as a possible framing issue for Ye, as well as unverified credit shares against ion-clock competitors.
responses.response: I think the comb overlap is a framing problem we can solve in the citation rather than a reason to hold back: the comb made optical frequencies countable, while the lattice clock solved a different problem, a many-atom interrogation free of Stark shifts at 1e-18. The ion-clock competitor point is harder, because Wineland's 2012 prize covered ion control and Al+ clocks are a parallel route. I would not want the citation to claim that lattice clocks are the only path to 1e-18. Danielsson's ranking of the Higgs trio without Della Negra also reinforces my worry about its attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
How much weight to give the pending redefinition of the second, and whether to wait for it.
Relative credit between Katori's concept and Ye's performance advances, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto or other lattice-clock groups need to be reflected.
Whether a principled and defensible three-person Higgs configuration exists, which would change my preference.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: none of the shortlisted candidates is a documented co-author, supervisor or colleague, and my work in turbulence, random matrices and neural networks does not overlap with the shortlisted fields. I note Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory link and Johansson's WACQT link as colleagues' own flags, not mine.
